name: Pixieset
tagline: Publish a simple password-protected client gallery from user-owned storage

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 3 GB storage; unlimited galleries; up to 3 mobile gallery apps; 15% store commission.

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: 10 GB storage; 30 minutes HD video; 100 email sends per month; unlimited mobile gallery apps; 0% Pixieset store commission.

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: 100 GB storage; 500 email sends per month; unlimited galleries and mobile apps; 0% Pixieset store commission.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: 1 TB storage; RAW-file support; unlimited galleries and mobile apps; 0% Pixieset store commission.

tiers.name: Ultimate
tiers.limits: Unlimited standard photo storage; 1,000 GB RAW-file cap; 10,000 email sends per month; 0% Pixieset store commission.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 3 GB storage, unlimited galleries, up to 3 mobile gallery apps and a 15% store commission
pricing.hiddenCosts: The Free store takes 15% of sales; extra video storage is $5/month per additional hour; Photo Editor is a separate $12/month add-on.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Pixieset, publish a simple password-protected client gallery from user-owned storage. The hard boundary is gallery hosting, proofing, downloads, store, mobile apps, and photographer workflow, plus image pipeline quality, models, and workflow polish.
coreLoopDIY: Catalog local photos, publish a password-protected client gallery from user-owned storage, generate previews, and export selected originals or rendered copies.
whatYouLose: gallery hosting, proofing, downloads, store, mobile apps, and photographer workflow
moatNotes: image pipeline quality, models, and workflow polish
ongoingBurden: raw codecs, color management, metadata, previews, face models, GPU support, storage, backups, sync, and export fidelity
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Pixieset because photographers pay because image quality, catalog safety, and fast handling of huge libraries matter more than cloning sliders. The recurring cost buys raw codecs, color management, metadata, previews, face models, GPU support, storage, backups, sync, and export fidelity, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Immich
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosted photo and video management platform.

alternatives.name: Lychee
alternatives.desc: A clean self-hosted gallery with password-protected albums, downloads, metadata, and Docker deployment; no built-in storefront.

alternatives.name: Piwigo
alternatives.desc: Private users and albums, passworded access, downloads, themes, and storage you own; less glossy, vastly less hostage-like.

rejectedAlternatives.name: CloudSpot Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Only three active galleries and downloads capped at 2048 pixels; fine for previews, not the promised client-delivery replacement.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Immich
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Great family photo server, awkward client gallery: sharing exists, but passworded proofing and presentation controls are not the product.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Pixieset Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Three gigabytes and platform branding make the free tier a sampler, while the more useful delivery controls remain paid.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Basic plan and a personal local photo catalog DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Pixieset in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, Rust image libraries, SQLite, and local filesystem access; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: catalog local photos, publish a password-protected client gallery from user-owned storage, generate previews, and export selected originals or rendered copies.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Index selected folders without moving or rewriting originals and store only catalog data in SQLite.
Generate thumbnails and previews, read EXIF, detect duplicates by hash, and monitor file changes.
Provide timeline, folders, albums, ratings, flags, tags, search, and side-by-side compare.
Store edits as reversible parameters for crop, rotate, exposure, contrast, white balance, and saturation.
Render exports to a new folder with explicit color space, quality, size, and metadata choices.
Add catalog backup, missing-file repair, integrity scan, and a clear original-safety guarantee.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a proprietary raw-rendering engine.
Deliberately leave out hosted cross-device photo sync and client galleries.
Deliberately leave out frontier culling, retouching, and generative models.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
